metadata.title: The Provincial and Federal Wedge Dividing BC's Sovereignty
metadata.fnfta_method: Compliance recomputed from the ISC/CIRNAC portal 'Date Received' for the audited statements and the Schedule of Remuneration. Deadline = fiscal year-end (Mar 31) + 120 days. compliant = both received by the deadline; late = both received after; partial = only one; none = neither. Portal shows the latest version received, so a re-filed document can show a later date. Bands that never filed in 12+ of 13 years are treated as likely exempt (treaty / self-governing) and excluded from the denominator.
sources: ISC/CIRNAC First Nation Profiles: FNFTA search (fnp-ppn.aadnc-aandc.gc.ca)
Canada Spends (canadaspends.com; X posts Feb 2026, Nov 2025)
Northern Beat (Rob Shaw; Public Land Use Society FOI; US-funding article)
Western Standard, 'EXCLUSIVE: Federal indigenous department admits it has no record of contact with BC's First Nations' (2026-06-08)
Cowichan Tribes v. Canada, 2025 BCSC 1490 (judgment text)
FNHA & BC PHO, Population Health and Wellness Agenda: First Interim Update (Aug 2024)
CBC News, 'First Nations life expectancy plunges by 6 years in B.C.: report' (Aug 21 2024)
Keith Wilson, X post 2025-11-07 (claim checked, not relied on)

cowichan.case: Cowichan Tribes v. Canada (Attorney General), 2025 BCSC 1490
held: The court found Aboriginal title over a portion of the claim area, called the Cowichan Title Lands (judgment para. 3724). The claim area is about 1,846 acres in Richmond; the judgment shows the title boundary on a map (Schedule A) and does not state its size in the text. Secondary reports put it at about 732 acres.

Crown grants of fee simple in the title lands 'unjustifiably infringe' Aboriginal title. Only specific Canada-owned and Richmond-owned lots (other than the YVR fuel project lands) were declared 'defective and invalid'; that declaration is suspended for 18 months (paras. 3638, 3724).

Privately held titles were not declared invalid: the plaintiffs did not seek that relief against private landowners, who are not parties (paras. 44, 2208). BC and Canada instead owe a duty to negotiate in good faith to reconcile those interests.

On coexistence the judge wrote that Aboriginal title and private fee simple titles 'will exist in the same land at the same time until future litigation or negotiation further modifies them and/or clarifies the practical aspect of the relationship' (para. 2208).
cowichan.appeal: All parties said they would appeal; BC stated 'a private property right sits above' Aboriginal title. A landowner (Montrose) bid to reopen was dismissed Jun 29 2026 and is itself under appeal. Status of the BC Court of Appeal hearing not confirmed.
cowichan.source: Judgment text, Cowichan Tribes v. Canada (Attorney General), 2025 BCSC 1490, read directly; appeal status and the ~732-acre figure come from secondary reports

claim_check.claim: 95% of BC land is under an Aboriginal title claim (Keith Wilson, Nov 2025)
claim_check.record: No BC government, BC Treaty Commission or court source located for the 95% figure. It appears to originate in this post. Asserted territories overlap heavily and many are untested, so a share of 'claimed' land depends on whose map is used; asserted is not proven.

claim_check.claim: Once Aboriginal title is established it trumps fee simple granted to landowners
claim_check.record: Cowichan (2025 BCSC 1490): Crown grants of fee simple in the title lands were found to unjustifiably infringe Aboriginal title, and only specific Canada- and Richmond-owned lots were declared invalid (suspended 18 months). No private title was voided: that relief was not sought, and the judge wrote that title and private fee simple 'will exist in the same land at the same time' until litigation or negotiation clarifies it (para. 2208). The parties announced appeals, and BC says private property sits above title.

claim_check.claim: BC residents may soon no longer own their homes and businesses
claim_check.record: Title was found over a portion of a 1,846-acre claim area of riverfront in Richmond (about 732 acres per secondary reports; the judgment shows a map, not a total). Private owners were not parties and no private title was declared invalid. The documented position is uncertainty until the appeals are decided; outcomes are not yet known.

claim_check.claim: Some 'First Nations' are First Nations only by name
claim_check.record: Documented: Coastal First Nations is an alliance of ~8-10 of ~70 coastal communities, set up in 2004 with US foundation money (Rockefeller Brothers Fund $1M + $100k start-up). It is an association, not an Indian Act band or treaty government. Band councils and treaty nations are separate legal entities. Evidence offered is from Vivian Krause's tax-document research as reported by Northern Beat.

claim_check.claim: George Soros funds the groups behind these agreements
claim_check.record: The cited Northern Beat article never mentions Soros. Documented funders there: Packard, Hewlett, Rockefeller Brothers, Moore, Tides Canada / MakeWay, Nature Conservancy, MacKenzie Scott. Open Society Foundations has given to the US Tides Foundation (amounts vary by source) but no OSF grant to a BC First Nation was found, and OSF denied funding Northern Gateway opposition in 2012.

claim_check.claim: CIRNAC has no record of contact with BC's First Nations
claim_check.record: Western Standard (Jun 8 2026): an ATIP request for a summary of the latest contact with each BC First Nation returned 'none responsive'. ATIP covers records that exist; a department need not create a spreadsheet. It shows no consolidated contact log, not that no contact occurred. Financial submissions via the portal are themselves a documented contact.

claim_check.claim: First Nations quality of life has been falling over the same decade that spending rose
claim_check.record: BC First Nations life expectancy peaked at 75.7 years (2011 and 2013), fell to 73.3 by 2019 (before the pandemic) and to 67.2 in 2021; mortality rose; diabetes rose. But the steep fall is 2020-21, which the health authorities attribute mainly to the toxic drug crisis and COVID-19 (other BC residents fell ~1 year over the same span). Several indicators improved (infant mortality, school completion, youth suicide). The data stops in 2021, and nothing here shows spending or reporting rules caused or failed to prevent the decline.

claim_check.claim: $243.8B has gone to First Nations groups
claim_check.record: $243.8B is cumulative federal 'Indigenous priorities' departmental spending 2014-2024 (Canada Spends), which includes health, housing, water, education, child welfare, land claims and settlement liabilities delivered to or for Indigenous people, not only transfers to band councils. Fraser's narrower inflation-adjusted series, excluding settlements, is $10.3B to $40.8B.

claim_check_2.claim: The federal fast-track law is Bill C-39, the Building Canada Act
claim_check_2.record: The law that lets 'designated projects' bypass some federal laws is Bill C-5. Coverage of the Oct 2026 Major Projects Office story describes it as Bill C-5.

claim_check_2.claim: The drinking-water settlement is $6.9B ($1.5B compensation plus $5.4B infrastructure)
claim_check_2.record: Reports put it at nearly $8B: $1.5B compensation, a $400M restoration fund and at least $6B for water systems.

claim_check_2.claim: The Supreme Court ruling resulted in the $10B Robinson Huron settlement
claim_check_2.record: The $10B ($5B each from Canada and Ontario) was settled before the July 2024 Restoule ruling. The ruling confirmed the Crown breached the treaties and left the Robinson Superior claim to be negotiated.

claim_check_2.claim: ISC demanded $12.3M from the FSIN and the FSIN filed a Federal Court judicial review
claim_check_2.record: ISC's March 2026 letter sought $28.7M after an audit flagged about $34M as questionable, ineligible or unsupported. The FSIN disputes it and says it will take legal action once chiefs give a mandate. No court filing or $12.3M figure was found.

Parliament does not vote on each settlement, and judgment payments can come from the Consolidated Revenue Fund without an appropriation. But settlement money still enters the Estimates (for example $5.0B for Restoule in Supplementary Estimates B 2023-24) and the liabilities are recorded in the Public Accounts.

claim_check_2.claim: Firms cancel major projects because of First Nations disputes and lawsuits
claim_check_2.record: Northern Gateway and Trans Mountain approvals were quashed over consultation. Energy East and Frontier were cancelled citing regulatory delay, markets and climate policy, not a First Nations ruling. Indigenous equity ownership has also enabled projects such as Cedar LNG.

claim_check_2.claim: A court let a First Nation's title claim proceed over land under a multibillion-dollar export facility
claim_check_2.record: The project and case were not named, and no matching case was found in the sources reviewed. The nearest documented examples are the Cowichan ruling (Richmond, with airport fuel lands carved out) and the Gitxaala mineral-claims ruling.

settlements.name: First Nations child welfare / Jordan's Principle
settlements.note: Covers children removed from homes on reserve or in Yukon, Apr 1 1991 to Mar 31 2022. Reported as $23.3B to $23.4B.

settlements.name: Robinson Huron treaty annuities
settlements.note: Annuity frozen at $4 per person since 1875. The Supreme Court (Restoule, July 2024) confirmed the Crown breached the treaties.

settlements.name: Drinking-water class action
settlements.note: Reported as nearly $8B: $1.5B compensation, a $400M restoration fund and at least $6B for water systems.

settlements.name: Gottfriedson (language and culture)
settlements.note: Paid to a trust run by a nine-member Indigenous board for 20 years; 325 First Nations in the class.

settlements.name: Treaty 9 annuities (Missanabie Cree class action)
settlements.note: Claim of at least $10B. Treaty 9 has no promise to raise annuities with resource wealth, so the argument differs from Robinson. Not a settlement.

public_money.pbo_supp_b_2023_24: PBO: Supplementary Estimates (B) 2023-24 included $5.0B for the Restoule Settlement Agreement, $1.6B for land-related claims and litigation and $596M for the Specific Claims Settlement Fund.
public_money.afr: Government of Canada Annual Financial Report 2023-24: over $60B provided since 2016 to resolve Indigenous claims; about $16.4B of 2023-24 expenses were Indigenous contingent liabilities.

fsin.fsin_position: Chief Bobby Cameron: 'We fully believe that we don't have to repay a dime'; legal action once chiefs give a mandate.

projects.stated_reason: Federal consultation with First Nations was inadequate. Neither the company nor Ottawa appealed.

projects.outcome: Approval quashed, later re-approved and built
projects.stated_reason: Inadequate consultation and exclusion of marine traffic from the regulator's review.
Company cited regulatory delay, cost and the scope of the review; the federal minister and some economists cited market conditions. No First Nations court ruling was involved.
Teck cited the absence of a framework reconciling resource development and climate policy. No First Nations court ruling was involved.

projects.outcome: Haisla Nation holds 50.1% equity; start-up expected 2027-28
projects.stated_reason: Counter-example: Indigenous equity ownership, financed in part by a $1.4B loan from the First Nations Finance Authority.

courts.gitxaala_bcca: Dec 5 2025 (2025 BCCA 430): the majority held DRIPA brings UNDRIP into BC law with immediate effect and found the online mineral-claim system inconsistent with it.
courts.scc_leave: The Gitxaala campaign page says the Supreme Court granted BC leave to appeal on May 21 2026, with a hearing expected in 2027.
courts.eby: Premier Eby called changing DRIPA 'non-negotiable' in April 2026. Search results later suggested a pivot to suspending key parts for three years; passage was not confirmed.
courts.mining_fraser: Fraser Institute commentary: BC mineral claims fell 29% in 2025 and claimed area 61% versus the seven-year average.
courts.mining_counter: The 2024 industry exploration survey (EY/AME) attributed a 14% fall in exploration spending partly to financing constraints and maturing projects; it predates the Gitxaala ruling.

overlaps.who: Nine Allied Tribes, Lax Kw'alaams, Wei Wai Kum vs the treaty nations and BC
overlaps.what: In April 2026 a coalition said it was ready to block major projects, including the corridors feeding the Port of Prince Rupert, and take legal action unless BC paused the treaties. They said the agreements reach into their territory and they were not consulted. Lax Kw'alaams said it does not oppose the treaty process itself.
overlaps.status: K'omoks Treaty Act passed on a free vote (May 2026 report); Kitselas Treaty Act not expected back for a vote until fall. BC's minister said overlap is not new and urged more talks.

overlaps.who: Cowichan Tribes, Stz'uminus, Penelakut, Halalt vs Musqueam and Tsawwassen
overlaps.what: Musqueam and Tsawwassen were two of six defendants opposing the claim. The court found the Cowichan's evidence of occupation more persuasive. Musqueam said it 'fundamentally disagrees' with the judgment. The judge wrote that all parties have continued interests around the south arm of the Fraser and that the findings will affect relationships among them (para. 3726).
overlaps.status: All parties have appealed; BC and Cowichan have begun negotiations.

overlaps.what: Gitanyow filed a 2003 claim to about 6,200 km2 that overlaps Nisga'a treaty lands; the Nisga'a were added as a party. Gitanyow argues overlaps must be resolved before treaties are concluded.
overlaps.status: Long-running; legal commentators count dozens of overlap cases tied to modern treaty negotiations.

overlaps.dispute: Tahltan vs Taku River Tlingit (Shesley River area)
overlaps.who: Tahltan Nation vs Taku River Tlingit First Nation
overlaps.what: After Taku River Tlingit declared an Indigenous protected area, the Tahltan said part of it, the Shesley River area, is Tahltan territory and that they had not consented (2024 report). The Tahltan also fully support the Eskay Creek mine, which Alaska tribal nations downstream have opposed.
overlaps.status: Tahltan said they would meet their neighbour. Eskay Creek has all permits and is targeting a 2027 restart.

overlaps.dispute: Wet'suwet'en hereditary chiefs vs elected councils
overlaps.who: Hereditary house chiefs vs elected band councils
overlaps.what: Two governance systems claim to speak for the same people. Eight of nine hereditary house chiefs opposed Coastal GasLink; 20 elected councils along the route signed benefits agreements. The Union of BC Indian Chiefs sided with the hereditary chiefs.
overlaps.status: Contested since 2019-20; elected chiefs also disputed the 2020 title memorandum between hereditary chiefs, Ottawa and BC.

overlaps.who: Okanagan Nation Alliance vs BC and Canada
overlaps.what: A civil claim challenging BC's treaty process over overlapping claims; the BC Treaty Commission's Chief Commissioner called for negotiation rather than litigation.
overlaps.status: Reported in the 2020s; current status not checked.

overlaps.who: Council of the Haida Nation, BC, Canada
overlaps.what: The 2024 Rising Tide agreement recognizes Haida title to Haida Gwaii. Its preamble states the Haida have no overlap with other Indigenous nations' interests on terrestrial Haida Gwaii; that is the Haida position written into the agreement, not a tribunal finding. No objection from other nations was found. Critics question how private land and parks fit.
overlaps.status: Provincial Act in force; a federal counterpart agreement followed in Feb 2025; transition issues remain.

overlap_context.scale: A University of Victoria source says every BC First Nation has at least one overlap area with another, because most nations never signed treaties.
overlap_context.ancillary: Overlap matters for the consent question: if two nations assert title to the same land, a deal with one can be challenged by the other.

bc_projects.stated_reason: The company cited changes in market conditions. Some Lax Kw'alaams members camped on the site for most of a year in protest, while leaders of other nearby nations supported the project. An industry CEO blamed delays by BC and Ottawa. BC's energy minister said it was global pricing.

bc_projects.outcome: Rejected twice by Ottawa (2010, 2014); courts upheld; final appeal refused 2020
bc_projects.stated_reason: A federal panel found significant, irreversible effects on water, fisheries and Tsilhqot'in cultural heritage. Taseko's court challenges failed; the Supreme Court refused leave in 2020.

bc_projects.outcome: Built; Treaty 8 challenges did not stop it
bc_projects.stated_reason: The Federal Court of Appeal and BC Court of Appeal dismissed challenges in early 2017. In 2018 the BC Supreme Court refused an injunction but ordered the Treaty 8 infringement claim to be tried. The final outcome of that trial was not confirmed.

Benefits agreements were signed with 20 elected band councils along the route; eight of nine Wet'suwet'en hereditary house chiefs opposed. The dispute is about who has authority, not only about the project.

bc_projects.outcome: Permitted in a first joint regulatory decision with the Tahltan Nation
bc_projects.stated_reason: Tahltan support the mine and co-decided on it. Alaska tribal nations downstream, who are not parties to the BC decision, have asked BC and Canada for recognition and a pause.

orgs.caveat: This is a high-level map from public documents, not a ranking. Funding is shown only where a public document gave it; 'not found' means the sources reviewed did not break it down.

groups.speaks_for: Their registered members on reserve and often off-reserve. The legal counterpart for most federal funding and programs.
groups.funding: Mainly federal transfers plus own-source revenue; they file the financial statements this report examines in sections 1-2.
groups.notes: In BC about 200 bands, many not covered by the transparency Act because of treaty or self-government.

groups.speaks_for: Their houses and clans, and in several cases the title-holding nation (for example the Wet'suwet'en).
groups.funding: Not found for the groups reviewed; the Office of the Wet'suwet'en was set up to represent the nation in treaty talks.
groups.notes: Contested alongside elected councils in the Wet'suwet'en case.

groups.group: Assembly of First Nations (AFN) and BC Assembly of First Nations (BCAFN)
groups.speaks_for: Chiefs of member First Nations (AFN: over 600 bands nationally; BCAFN is the BC regional body).
groups.funding: Audited statements are adopted by the chiefs in assembly (BCAFN's 2024-25 statements by KPMG, Oct 2025). Revenue by source was not found in the documents reviewed.
groups.notes: Speaks for governments, not individual members.

groups.group: First Nations Summit and Union of BC Indian Chiefs (UBCIC)
groups.speaks_for: The Summit: about 150 First Nations taking part, focused on the treaty process. UBCIC (founded 1969): nations that reject the current treaty process and defend title and rights.
groups.notes: With the BCAFN they form the First Nations Leadership Council under a 2005 accord. Some bands belong to more than one.

groups.kind: Service organization created by tripartite agreement (2011)
groups.speaks_for: BC First Nations for health governance and delivery.
groups.funding: Federal funding agreement of roughly $380 million a year for 2013-2023 (about $4.7 billion), plus BC support.
groups.notes: A public service body, not an advocacy group.

groups.group: Coastal First Nations - Great Bear Initiative
groups.speaks_for: Nine to ten member First Nations on the north and central coast and Haida Gwaii. Its board has one representative from each member.
groups.funding: Grants and contributions of $16.9 million in the year to March 2022 (from $10.6 million in FY2020). Partners named: governments of Canada and BC, Coast Funds, BC Hydro, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, MakeWay, the Wilburforce Foundation, Nature United, The Nature Conservancy, Rogers and others. The split by funder was not given.
groups.notes: An alliance of First Nation governments, not a nation or band itself. It is not 'in name only', but it is a mixed public and private-philanthropy funded body.

groups.speaks_for: Nearly 85 member nations, mostly in BC, seeking equity in major projects.
groups.funding: Federal: $2.6 million (2021) and $13.5 million (2022) from Natural Resources Canada. It backed the federal Indigenous loan guarantee program.
groups.notes: Supports Indigenous ownership of resource projects.

groups.group: Indian Resource Council and National Coalition of Chiefs
groups.speaks_for: The IRC advocates federal policy to expand First Nations economic development (led by Stephen Buffalo). The Coalition: 50-plus chiefs and Metis leaders who opposed Bill C-69 and Bill C-48.
groups.funding: Not found. Much coverage comes from think-tank commentary, so treat framing as advocacy.

groups.group: Indigenous-led environmental groups and funders (for example Raven Trust, Indigenous Climate Action, Tides Canada / MakeWay)
groups.speaks_for: Their own boards and supporters, often alongside affected nations.
groups.funding: Foundations such as Rockefeller Brothers, Moore, Packard, Hewlett and the Nature Conservancy, per the Northern Beat reporting used in section 7. Grant-level records are in public tax filings but were not compiled here.
groups.notes: Foreign philanthropy is lawful and reported; whether it should shape land-use talks is a political question.

foreign_funding.source: Northern Beat (Rob Shaw/ staff), 'US money behind anti-resource activism in BC', citing Vivian Krause's US tax-filing research
foreign_funding.reliability_note: Northern Beat is an advocacy-leaning outlet and Krause's work is contested. The underlying filings (US Form 990s, Canadian charity returns) are public and should be checked at source.

documented.item: Rockefeller Brothers Fund: $1M capital + $100k start-up for Coastal First Nations (2004)
Moore Foundation: ~$270M into Canadian activism since 2000s, ~$30M to Coastal First Nations, ~$85M via Tides Canada (incl. $10M grant, 2015)
Great Bear Rainforest fund (2007): $120M total, $30M federal share; US donors named: Packard, Wilberforce, Hewlett, Rockefeller Brothers, Moore
MakeWay (formerly Tides Canada): $86M from MacKenzie Scott since 2022
Coast Economic Development Society + related society: $120M annual revenue and endowment, private donors plus BC and federal subsidies

context: Funding to First Nation-led conservation is lawful and charitable-sector transparent; the question raised is who sets land-use agenda when external funds shape negotiation tables.

timeline_events.event: First Nations Financial Transparency Act passes (S.C. 2013, c. 7): bands must publish audited statements and a remuneration schedule within 120 days of year-end
Minister Bennett ends discretionary compliance measures; ~$12M withheld from ~43 bands is reinstated; court actions suspended
BC Provincial Health Officer declares the toxic drug (overdose) public health emergency
National Post: 85% of bands still compliant for the last year, versus 90%+ while funding was at stake
